props.title: Kansas City
props.initialSlug: Jazz, crime and politics collide in 1930s KC

sections.content: Robert Altman's Kansas City stands as a gritty jazz-noir that captures both the political machinations and musical innovation of Depression-era Missouri. The film weaves together the stories of Blondie O'Hara (Jennifer Jason Leigh) and Carolyn Stilton (Miranda Richardson) against the backdrop of the 1934 Kansas City jazz scene. Like Altman's masterpiece Nashville (1975), it uses music as both setting and metaphor, with extended jazz sequences at the Hey Hey Club featuring recreations of legendary performances by Coleman Hawkins and Lester Young. The film's structure mirrors the improvisational nature of jazz itself, with intersecting storylines that build like instrumental solos.

sections.content: Altman's attention to historical detail in Kansas City extends beyond the music. The film meticulously recreates the corrupt political machine of Tom Pendergast, showing how jazz flourished alongside gambling, bootlegging, and vote-buying. This political backdrop echoes similar themes in Altman's Short Cuts (1993) and Nashville (1975), where music becomes inextricable from power structures. The Hey Hey Club scenes, featuring contemporary musicians playing period pieces, create a documentary-like authenticity that rivals Straight No Chaser (1988) and Let's Get Lost (1988). SUBHEAD: Jazz in American Cinema

The film sits within a rich tradition of jazz-centered American cinema, from New York, New York (1977) to 'Round Midnight (1986). What distinguishes Kansas City is its focus on the territorial bands and swing era that preceded bebop. While films like Lady Sings the Blues (1972) and Bird (1988) explore the personal torments of jazz icons, Altman uses jazz as a lens to examine broader social and political dynamics. The film's recreation of the Hey Hey Club becomes a microcosm of Depression-era race relations and class struggles.
